reference.source: Textbook of Autoinflammation / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A recessive histiocytic disorder caused by mutations in SLC29A3, which encodes an equilibrative nucleoside transporter
Named for its recurring features, many beginning with the letter H, including hyperpigmentation, hypertrichosis, and hearing loss
Characteristic cutaneous change is indurated, hyperpigmented, hypertrichotic skin, often over the inner thighs and lower body, sparing certain areas
Systemic features include hepatosplenomegaly, heart anomalies, hypogonadism, low height (short stature), and insulin-dependent diabetes
Histology shows infiltration by histiocytes, placing it within the spectrum of non-Langerhans histiocytoses
It overlaps clinically and genetically with other SLC29A3-related conditions and can mimic Rosai-Dorfman disease
Management is largely supportive and directed at individual organ complications, as no single curative therapy exists
reference.pathophysiology: H syndrome is caused by biallelic mutations in SLC29A3, encoding the equilibrative nucleoside transporter hENT3 that moves nucleosides across intracellular membranes, particularly in lysosomes of macrophages. Loss of transporter function disturbs nucleoside handling and macrophage homeostasis, promoting accumulation and activation of histiocytes. The resulting tissue infiltration by histiocytes produces the cutaneous, endocrine, and systemic manifestations. Because the underlying process is a histiocytic infiltration with autoinflammatory features rather than a single cytokine defect, treatment is directed at complications and inflammation as they arise.
additionalDifferentials: Other SLC29A3 spectrum disorders (e.g. PHID, Faisalabad histiocytosis)
Scleroderma or scleredema affecting the skin
Systemic lupus erythematosus with cutaneous change
additionalInvestigations: Endocrine assessment including glucose and gonadal function
redFlags: New endocrine failure such as insulin-dependent diabetes
Features suggesting malignant transformation within histiocytic disease
reference.prognosis: H syndrome is a chronic multisystem disorder; life expectancy can be relatively preserved but morbidity accrues from progressive skin, endocrine, sensorineural, and organ involvement requiring long-term multidisciplinary care.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the skin changes as scleroderma and missing the histiocytic aetiology
Failing to recognise the association with insulin-dependent diabetes and hearing loss
Overlooking overlap with Rosai-Dorfman disease and related SLC29A3 disorders
Not pursuing genetic testing in a child with hyperpigmented, hypertrichotic indurated skin
management: Direct anti-inflammatory therapy at active histiocytic and autoinflammatory disease with corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppressants, with the anti-interleukin-6 agent tocilizumab reported to be beneficial
Manage insulin-dependent diabetes with insulin and structured endocrine follow-up
Support sensorineural hearing loss with audiology input and hearing aids
Address hypogonadism and short stature with endocrine review and hormone replacement as indicated
Evaluate and manage structural and valvular cardiac anomalies
Provide multidisciplinary long-term surveillance of the skin, endocrine, cardiac, hepatic and auditory systems
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive SLC29A3-related inheritance with family testing
